identity.title: Seizure-vs-syncope features: prolonged (>1-5 min) post-event confusion, lateral tongue biting, head turning, incontinence

technique.how: Ask a witness how long the patient was confused or disoriented after regaining consciousness (minutes vs seconds) and whether they saw head turning or sustained tonic posturing; inspect the tongue for a lateral laceration and ask about incontinence. Record the patient's own recall of events immediately before and after.
technique.prerequisites: An eyewitness account is needed for post-event orientation and motor features; the tongue must be examined directly.

interpretation.positive_finding: Disorientation after the event (LR ~5) or a lateral tongue bite (specificity 0.96-1.0) strongly favours an epileptic seizure over syncope.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of tongue biting barely lowers seizure probability (LR- ~0.7, sensitivity 0.24-0.33); brief confusion is compatible with either.
interpretation.pitfalls: Brief myoclonic jerks and a few seconds of confusion are common in convulsive syncope; incontinence and trauma did not discriminate in Hoefnagels 1991. Tip-of-tongue bites occur in syncope, so laterality matters.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: pursue seizure work-up (EEG, imaging, neurology) rather than cardiac syncope pathway; negative: does not exclude seizure.

estimates.target_condition: Epileptic seizure vs syncope as cause of transient loss of consciousness (finding: disorientation immediately after the event, per eyewitness)
estimates.population: 94 consecutive patients aged >=15 with transient loss of consciousness (41 seizure, 53 syncope)
estimates.reference_standard: Eyewitnessed clonic movements or automatisms classified as seizure; remainder syncope/related; likelihood ratios computed by authors
estimates.quote: We found a seizure five times more likely than syncope if the patient was disoriented after the event

estimates.target_condition: Epileptic seizure vs syncope (finding: any tongue biting)
estimates.population: Pooled 2 studies: 75 patients with epileptic seizures and 98 with syncope
estimates.reference_standard: Video-EEG-documented seizures vs clinically/tilt-diagnosed syncope in the primary studies
estimates.quote: sensitivity 33%, specificity 96%, pLR 8.167 (95% CI 2.969-22.461) and nLR 0.695 (95% CI 0.589-0.82)

estimates.target_condition: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure vs nonepileptic event/syncope (finding: any tongue biting)
estimates.population: 63 epilepsy-monitoring-unit patients with bilateral motor activity and/or loss of consciousness (34 epileptic, 29 nonepileptic) plus 45 syncope patients
estimates.reference_standard: Video-EEG monitoring (epileptic vs nonepileptic); syncope cohort by clinical diagnosis
estimates.quote: Tongue biting had a sensitivity of 24% and a specificity of 99% for the diagnosis of generalized tonic-clonic seizures.

estimates.target_condition: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure (finding: LATERAL tongue biting)
estimates.population: Same cohort as above (63 monitored patients + 45 syncope patients)
estimates.reference_standard: Video-EEG monitoring; syncope cohort by clinical diagnosis
estimates.quote: Lateral tongue biting was 100% specific to grand mal seizures.

sources.citation: Hoefnagels WA, Padberg GW, Overweg J, van der Velde EA, Roos RA. Transient loss of consciousness: the value of the history for distinguishing seizure from syncope. J Neurol. 1991;238(1):39-43.
Brigo F, Nardone R, Bongiovanni LG. Value of tongue biting in the differential diagnosis between epileptic seizures and syncope. Seizure. 2012;21(8):568-572.
Benbadis SR, Wolgamuth BR, Goren H, Brener S, Fouad-Tarazi F. Value of tongue biting in the diagnosis of seizures. Arch Intern Med. 1995;155(21):2346-2349.
Sheldon R, Rose S, Ritchie D, et al. Historical criteria that distinguish syncope from seizures. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2002;40(1):142-148.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on these features to exclude cardiac syncope in a patient with structural heart disease or an abnormal ECG; convulsive syncope from asystole or VT can mimic seizure.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Prolonged confusion that does not resolve, focal deficits, fever or head trauma require urgent evaluation for status epilepticus, stroke or CNS infection.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Post-event orientation depends on an eyewitness; patient self-report of confusion duration is unreliable. Tongue inspection is objective.

extraction_notes: Anchor (Sheldon 2002, PMID 12103268) is not open access; abstract gives only the composite point score (94% sens/spec) and no per-item numbers, so it is cited but no estimate is taken from it. Post-event disorientation LR is entered as 5 from the Hoefnagels 1991 abstract wording 'five times more likely' (authors state likelihood ratios were used); no CI available. Prevalence 0.44 = 41/94 from abstract counts. Tongue biting: pooled Brigo 2012/2013 meta-analysis (2 studies; PubMed lists year 2013, journal issue 2012) and the Benbadis 1995 primary study (any vs lateral tongue bite entered separately). Hoefnagels 1991 abstract states incontinence and trauma were not discriminative - recorded in pitfalls, no number. Head turning was not quantified in any accessible source.
